answerEvidence.summary: Reader on the RG scope inherits to all current and future resources per scope-overview parent-child hierarchy while granting only read-only management via built-in Reader.

distractorEvidence.summary: Subscription-scope Reader inherits down to every RG in the subscription, exceeding the Finance-only requirement per scope-overview.
Built-in Contributor grants resource management writes, which the auditor is not permitted to receive.
Assignments on individually enumerated resources do not carry to separately created future resources; scope-overview inheritance runs top-down, not sibling to sibling.

rubric.notes: Applied difficulty is closer to intermediate scope selection than a boss reasoning question, but scenario is complete with resource-inheritance nuance and future-resource clause. Distractors realistically model over-scoping, excess-write, and static-enumeration mistakes. Documentation strength is high with two directly aligned articles.

answerEvidence.summary: RBAC overview Multiple role assignments example: subscription Contributor sums with a narrower Reader to yield Contributor; Reader has no impact.

distractorEvidence.summary: RBAC overview describes narrower assignments as considered alongside inherited assignments, not categorically ignored.
Reader is read-only and does not carry role-assignment privileges to remove; and Contributor itself excludes role assignment via NotActions.
Group and direct assignments are combined additively, not prioritized by source.

rubric.notes: Additive-model troubleshooting fits AZ-104 intermediate level. Options exercise the widespread misconception that a narrower Reader restricts inherited Contributor. Explanations cite the exact Multiple role assignments example. Wording is neutral and testable without extra context.

answerEvidence.summary: Effect-basics states each assignment is independently evaluated and the cumulative most restrictive assignment applies; deny at subscription blocks a non-eastus2 request even when child audit does not object.

distractorEvidence.summary: Effect-basics does not describe more-specific audits as replacements for inherited deny assignments.
Deny only rejects noncompliant requests; effect-basics separately documents modify effects for property adjustments.
Different allowed regions do not disable enforcement; deny remains deny per effect-basics evaluation order.

rubric.notes: Policy layering scenario with two allowed-region mismatches mirrors the effect-basics worked example. Distractors reflect real misreadings (child overrides, deny as modify, audit-only). Difficulty maps well to advanced-tier applied reasoning.

answerEvidence.summary: CanNotDelete permits reads and modifications while blocking deletes; applied to the RG it inherits to its resources without preventing authorized updates.

distractorEvidence.summary: ReadOnly limits authorized users to Reader-equivalent access, blocking VM size and configuration updates.
Moving ReadOnly to VMs still blocks the required configuration updates on those VMs.
Configure locks note explicitly forbids adding a lock at management-group scope.

rubric.notes: Beginner-level lock selection remains authentic because the management-group scope distractor probes a common misconception; overall a bit easier than advertised difficulty but still legitimate concept recall with implementation implication.

answerEvidence.summary: Replacing the RG lock with CanNotDelete keeps group-wide deletion protection (inheritance) while allowing VM start and List Keys POSTs; storage account still has its own CanNotDelete, and SAS overview shows uploads are data-plane and unaffected.

distractorEvidence.summary: Locks override user permissions per lock-resources; adding Owner does not remove an inherited ReadOnly.
Removing the RG lock leaves other resources in the group unprotected against deletion, violating the group-wide requirement.
Removing only the storage account lock leaves ReadOnly on the RG, which still blocks VM start and List Keys per the article examples.

rubric.notes: Expert-tier scenario integrates lock inheritance (most restrictive wins), blocked POST operations (VM start, List Keys), the data-plane bypass for SAS uploads, and the fact that Owner does not bypass locks. Distractors are documentation-grounded and each removes a documented protection.

answerEvidence.summary: Selected with a nesting parent group is the documented pilot pattern because the admin center supports one selected group and SSPR resolves nested groups.

distractorEvidence.summary: All enables SSPR tenant-wide, expanding the pilot beyond the two permitted groups; registration prompts are separate from enablement scope.
The tutorial documents Microsoft Entra admin center as supporting selection of only one group at a time.
None disables SSPR for the tenant; registration does not enable users whose scope is None.

rubric.notes: Genuine intermediate SSPR pilot design question that exploits the admin-center single-group limit and nested-group support. Distractors reflect realistic misconceptions about All/None and multi-group selection. Documentation is a single authoritative tutorial.

answerEvidence.summary: Assignment managed identity performs the deployment; per the note under Configure the managed identity, roleDefinitionIds edits require manual role grants on that identity, even in the portal.

distractorEvidence.summary: Administrator privileges do not become the managed identity permissions used for remediation.
The article states managed identity location does not affect Policy operation.
Re-evaluation is not a role grant; Changing a policy definition does not automatically update the associated managed identity per the boxed note.

rubric.notes: Advanced-tier troubleshooting that separates evaluation identity from remediation identity and pins down the edit-roleDefinitionIds warning. Distractor set covers admin-vs-identity confusion, managed-identity location myth and re-evaluation misconception.

answerEvidence.summary: User delegation SAS is signed with the user delegation key obtained with Microsoft Entra credentials, avoiding possession of an account key.

distractorEvidence.summary: Storage-sas describes account SAS as signed with the storage account key regardless of the service subset.
Service SAS is signed with the account key with or without a stored access policy.
Short expiry does not change the account-key signing requirement of an ad hoc service SAS.

rubric.notes: Beginner SAS-type selection with a precise no-account-key constraint. Distractors keep the account-key signing tie visible. Difficulty is beginner-appropriate; overall assessment remains strong on documentation and uniqueness.

answerEvidence.summary: Storage-sas describes a service SAS associated with a container stored access policy that inherits its constraints and supports revocation without regenerating account keys.

distractorEvidence.summary: Ad hoc tokens embed their constraints in the URI; tracking them elsewhere does not create server-side revocation control.
Storage-sas note explicitly states an account SAS must be ad hoc and cannot use a stored access policy.
Shortening future token expiries does not modify the permissions already granted to distributed tokens.

rubric.notes: Solid intermediate design question that isolates stored access policy revocation semantics and rejects the impossible account-SAS-with-stored-policy trap. Explanations use the article language accurately.

answerEvidence.summary: RA-GZRS supplies zone-redundant primary-region availability plus read access to the asynchronously replicated secondary without failover, accepting replication lag.

distractorEvidence.summary: GZRS without read access does not expose the secondary for reads until a failover is initiated per Read access to data in the secondary region.
RA-GRS replicates within the primary region using LRS, not ZRS, so a primary-zone outage can interrupt reads and writes.
ZRS alone has no geographically separate secondary region for reads during a regional outage.

rubric.notes: Expert-tier redundancy design correctly separates zone-level availability, read access to secondary, and asynchronous lag. Distractors model realistic confusion between RA-GRS and RA-GZRS as well as GZRS reads before failover.

answerEvidence.summary: Blob tiering states rehydration alone does not trigger object replication and that replication requires a subsequent data update on the source blob once both copies are online.

distractorEvidence.summary: Replication rules subsection states write operations to the destination container are not permitted while replication is active and return 409 Conflict.
Blob tiering explicitly requires a data update, and the article notes source-tier changes do not change destination tier.
Blob versioning subsection states versioning cannot be disabled while an object-replication policy is in effect.

rubric.notes: Expert troubleshooting requires knowing that rehydration does not trigger replication and that a source data update is required, together with the destination-write and versioning prerequisites. Distractors are grounded in the article.

answerEvidence.summary: Overwrites with soft delete on create a soft-deleted snapshot; restoration is Undelete Blob followed by copying the desired snapshot over the base blob to promote it.

distractorEvidence.summary: Undelete restores blobs and snapshots but does not automatically promote a snapshot to replace the surviving base blob.
Versioning enabled retroactively does not create a version of a prior overwrite; the article covers the versionless overwrite path.
Soft-deleted data cannot be read without first restoring it, and disabling soft delete does not perform that restoration.

rubric.notes: Advanced technical implementation isolates the two-step Undelete-and-copy promotion. The versioning-off precondition is explicit, and distractors reflect realistic misuse of Undelete and disabling soft delete.

answerEvidence.summary: Only the blob matching both prefix and tag filters is selected, and the lifecycle delete action honors soft delete by moving it to the soft-deleted state for the configured retention.

distractorEvidence.summary: Lifecycle Known issues state the delete action places matching blobs into the soft-deleted state when soft delete is enabled instead of permanent deletion.
Filters are combined with logical AND per the rule element table; matching only one filter does not select the blob.
Soft delete does not prevent lifecycle delete from acting on current matching blobs; it changes the outcome to soft-deleted retention.

rubric.notes: Well-formed advanced question combining AND filter semantics with soft-delete integration. Both cited articles independently support the answer. Distractors challenge OR-filter, immediate-delete and soft-delete-blocks-rules myths.

answerEvidence.summary: Incremental mode reapplies the complete set of properties for included resources and resets omitted properties to defaults, so the fix is to include all required non-default properties.

distractorEvidence.summary: Complete mode deletes resources not present in the template and does not perform property-merge behavior on included resources.
Deployment-modes explicitly refutes partial-property incremental merging.
Removing the resource leaves it unchanged in incremental mode, so the intended update is not applied.

rubric.notes: Advanced ARM implementation directly targets the properties-are-reapplied-not-merged pitfall and the complete-mode deletion risk. Explanation is aligned to the article wording. Distractors are calibrated to real deployment mistakes.

answerEvidence.summary: dependsOn on the network interface with a resourceId expression makes the interface wait for the referenced virtual network per the resource-dependency example.

distractorEvidence.summary: The dependsOn array explicitly accepts resource names or IDs including resourceId expressions, so the dependency edge is honored.
The dependsOn belongs to the network interface, so the interface depends on the network, not the reverse.
Independent resources deploy in parallel; one dependency does not force JSON textual serial ordering across the template.

rubric.notes: Intermediate code-interpretation question mapping the dependsOn direction onto real deployment behavior. Fragment matches the article example; distractors capture common misreadings around resourceId, direction, and text-order sequencing.

answerEvidence.summary: Temporary disks use platform-managed keys while OS and data disk caches inherit the customer-managed key type from their managed disks.

distractorEvidence.summary: Temporary disks are always encrypted with platform-managed keys regardless of the disk key type.
When the disk is encrypted with customer-managed keys the cache for the disk uses customer-managed keys, per the intro paragraph.
The article states temporary disks are encrypted at rest with platform-managed keys, not left unencrypted.

rubric.notes: Advanced scenario carefully separates temporary-disk PMK from cache CMK inheritance. Distractors capture realistic over-generalizations about CMK coverage and unencrypted temp disks.

answerEvidence.summary: Resize is disruptive, cluster availability may require deallocation, OS and data disks persist and deallocation releases dynamic IPs per the article.

distractorEvidence.summary: Regional availability does not guarantee the current hardware cluster supports the size; deallocation may still be required.
Stopping only the guest OS leaves the VM on the same allocated hardware cluster, which cannot supply the size.
Deallocating a VM releases its dynamic public IP address; the address is not guaranteed to persist across allocation.

rubric.notes: Intermediate resize planning correctly integrates cluster availability, restart behavior, dynamic-IP release and disk persistence. Distractors probe the common myth that regional availability equals cluster availability and that dynamic IPs survive deallocation.

answerEvidence.summary: OnFailure is the only policy documented to restart specifically on nonzero exit codes while leaving successful completion stopped.

distractorEvidence.summary: Always restarts containers on successful completion as well, contradicting the desire to stop after a zero-exit success.
Never only guarantees no restart on zero exit; the platform can still restart the container on nonzero exit codes per the article.

rubric.notes: Beginner ACI restart-policy selection but includes the current documentation caveat about Never permitting platform restarts on nonzero exits, which raises rigor above trivial recall. Three-option format keeps it authentic.

answerEvidence.summary: CLI or ARM is required for managed-identity authentication on a Service Bus scale rule with single revision mode; minReplicas remains zero to satisfy scale-to-zero.

distractorEvidence.summary: The default HTTP rule cannot wake a zero-replica worker on Service Bus messages when ingress is disabled per the closing note.
Setting minReplicas to 1 violates the explicit zero-instance idle requirement.
Configuring a connection-string secret violates the no-stored-secrets requirement even though scale-app supports secret-based authentication.

rubric.notes: Expert Container Apps troubleshooting combines the zero-ingress scale-to-zero warning, single revision requirement for non-HTTP rules and portal managed-identity limitation. Distractors each violate one required constraint, keeping uniqueness sharp.

answerEvidence.summary: Marking the connection string as a Deployment slot setting preserves per-slot database targets while a same-direction re-swap performs the requested content rollback.

distractorEvidence.summary: Slot host names do not make an unmarked connection string sticky; unmarked connection strings swap with the content.
Overwriting both slots with the test setting eliminates the production database configuration.
Deleting the staging slot removes the retained previous production content that enables the slot-based rollback.

rubric.notes: Advanced slot design cleanly separates per-slot database configuration from content swapping and uses the same-direction re-swap rollback pattern documented for slots. Distractors capture realistic misconfigurations.

answerEvidence.summary: Private endpoint provides inbound isolation once public access is disabled, VNet integration in a separate subnet supplies outbound to the private database, and DNS resolves the app privately.

distractorEvidence.summary: VNet integration is outbound only per overview-vnet-integration and provides no private inbound path to the app.
App Service private endpoints are documented as inbound-only per overview-private-endpoint and do not carry outbound app calls.
Private-endpoint article requires a different subnet from VNet integration and states public access must be explicitly disabled to isolate the app.

rubric.notes: Expert architecture question rigorously separates inbound private endpoint, outbound VNet integration, subnet separation and explicit public-access disablement. Two authoritative articles jointly support the answer.

answerEvidence.summary: Rules are processed in priority order lowest first and processing stops on match, so priority 220 denies the connection.

distractorEvidence.summary: Lower numbers are higher priority; a larger priority number is not preferred.
A later matching allow does not override an earlier matching deny; processing stops at the first match.
Only identical priority and direction is a conflict; the two shown rules differ in priority and coexist.

rubric.notes: Beginner recall of priority ordering but includes the common myth that higher numbers or later allows win, making it more instructive than pure trivia. Exclusion of security admin rules keeps the answer unique.

answerEvidence.summary: NSG flow records are stateful; rule changes affect only new connections, so the current SSH session survives while new attempts are denied.

distractorEvidence.summary: The stateful behavior applies to TCP and UDP flows alike per the flow-record paragraph.
DenyAllInbound at 65500 is the default, and no default rule provides internet-to-SSH allow.
Existing flow records preserve state; they do not create replacement NSG rules.

rubric.notes: Intermediate stateful-NSG troubleshooting anchored in the documented SSH example. Distractors realistically model TCP-vs-UDP, default-rule confusion, and misinterpreting flow records as rule mutations.

answerEvidence.summary: Longest prefix wins first so BGP /24 beats UDR /0, and equal-prefix tie-breaking by source only applies for identical prefixes.

distractorEvidence.summary: For equal prefixes the documented order is user-defined then BGP then system, not BGP first.
A UDR 0.0.0.0/0 default route can match private and public addresses alike; the routing article does not carve out private destinations.
The article specifies a most-specific-route decision, not load balancing across unequal prefixes.

rubric.notes: Advanced routing troubleshooting isolates longest-prefix precedence over route-source tie-breaking. The scenario excludes preferred and service-endpoint routes to keep uniqueness. Distractors reflect widespread BGP-vs-UDR misconceptions.

answerEvidence.summary: Linking without autoregistration makes the network a resolution network whose VMs query zone records without registering their own names.

distractorEvidence.summary: Autoregistration would automatically create records for both existing and new VMs in the linked network, violating the requirement.
Only one link between a private DNS zone and a given virtual network is supported per Other considerations.
Without a link, VMs in the network cannot resolve records in the private zone regardless of manually created records.

rubric.notes: Intermediate DNS link design correctly separates registration and resolution behavior and rejects the multi-link myth. Documentation is a single authoritative article.

answerEvidence.summary: IPv4 probes originate from 168.63.129.16 and must be permitted in both NSGs and local firewall policies, so allowing that source in the guest firewall unblocks the probe.

distractorEvidence.summary: Changing the probe interval does not make the local firewall accept the blocked source address.
The documented probe source is 168.63.129.16, not the load-balancer frontend public IP.
The NSG already permits AzureLoadBalancer probes and client access is working; the failure is in the guest firewall, not NSG client rules.

rubric.notes: Advanced probe troubleshooting matches capture, listener and NSG state to isolate the local firewall as the failure. Answer requires knowing the 168.63.129.16 IPv4 source; distractors probe misconceptions about probe source and interval tuning.

answerEvidence.summary: A scheduled alert processing rule scoped to the maintenance RG suppresses action groups while the fired alerts remain visible, matching the documented maintenance pattern.

distractorEvidence.summary: Disabling the alert rules stops them firing and, being shared, also silences resources outside maintenance.
Deleting shared action groups affects unrelated resources and is not the scheduled scoped suppression control offered by the feature.
An unfiltered subscription scope suppresses notifications for resources that must keep notifying normally.

rubric.notes: Intermediate implementation of maintenance suppression correctly leverages scoped scheduled processing rules and preserves visibility of fired alerts. Distractors realistically over-suppress shared resources.

answerEvidence.summary: Two Log Analytics workspaces require two settings, and storage can be added to one of them since a setting may hold one destination of each type.

distractorEvidence.summary: A single setting cannot include two destinations of the same type per the requirements bullet.
One setting may fan out to multiple destination types, so a third setting is unnecessary for the mixed workspace-plus-storage design.
Resource logs are not collected by default; diagnostic settings must select and route them.

rubric.notes: Advanced routing design of diagnostic settings uses the exact documented per-type destination limit. Distractors probe over-fanout and no-fanout myths and the default-collection misconception.

answerEvidence.summary: Undelete restores the soft-deleted backup item and its retained restore points, permitting Restore VM from that data as documented in the portal steps.

distractorEvidence.summary: Retention configuration is not the item-recovery operation; the documented step is Undelete first.
Resume backup only after Undelete returns the item to Stop protection with retain data per the documented flow.
The article states retained restore points are used for the restore operation after Undelete; a fresh backup is not a prerequisite.

rubric.notes: Beginner recovery sequence but Undelete-first before restore is a nuance many miss under pressure. Distractors reflect realistic missteps such as extending retention or resuming without Undelete.

answerEvidence.summary: Latest processed uses the most recent recovery point already processed by Site Recovery and does not spend time processing additional received data, matching the stated priority.

distractorEvidence.summary: Latest first processes all data sent to Site Recovery to build a fresh recovery point before failover, which the scenario explicitly rules out.
Latest app-consistent chooses the latest application-consistent point, which the scenario says it does not require.
Latest multi-VM app-consistent targets multi-VM consistency groups and enforces application consistency, neither of which is required here.

rubric.notes: Intermediate Site Recovery scenario carefully pairs the requested priority (RTO, no additional processing, no app-consistent) with the Latest processed recovery point option, and distractors match documented alternatives.
